sense: the people living in a place, and their number

terms.gloss: the population: the number of people
evidence: Liv. 1.44.3: ad eam multitūdinem urbs quoque amplificanda vīsa est
Traupman 205, 363: population; numerus omnis multitūdinis, the total population
terms.comment: Livy’s word for the people a city holds, or hopes to hold; with numerus for the figure.
Lewis & Short: an inhabitant, a resident, as against a citizen. Morgan–Owens counts a population as the number of its inhabitants.

terms.gloss: the Roman census: the count of the citizens and their property
evidence: Liv. 1.44.2: mīlia octōgintā eō lūstrō cīvium cēnsa dīcuntur
terms.comment: Taken by the censors every five years and closed by the purification, the lūstrum (Lewis & Short); the result is given as cēnsa cīvium capita, the citizens counted (Liv. 3.24.10). Caesar uses the word for a count of the Helvetii.

terms.gloss: a count of the people; a census
evidence: Suet. Caes. 41.3: recēnsum populī … vīcātim per dominōs īnsulārum ēgit
terms.comment: Post-Augustan: Caesar’s street-by-street count of the people who drew free grain. Traupman’s word for a modern census.
A false friend: from populor, “lay waste”. The sense “population” is late Latin, in one poet (Sedulius, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Mīlia octōgintā eō lūstrō cīvium cēnsa dīcuntur … Ad eam multitūdinem urbs quoque amplificanda vīsa est.
phrases.english: Eighty thousand citizens are said to have been counted at that census … For a population of that size the city, too, seemed to need enlarging.

phrases.latin: cum in spem magis futūrae multitūdinis quam ad id quod tum hominum erat mūnīrent
phrases.english: for they built their walls for the population they hoped for rather than for the people they had then

lustrum.html: De Vaan, s.v. lūstrum, “ceremony of purification; five-year period”, from *luH- “set free” (luō); distinct from lustrum, a muddy place, a den.
